item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q006_ubiquitin_like_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places ubiquitin-related proteins, UBX domains, and Ras-binding domains in distinct families within the ubiquitin-like superfamily of the beta-grasp fold (SCOPe d.15.1 within fold d.15, an alpha+beta class). This supports remote homology—a shared ancestral structural core—more strongly than a mere same-fold resemblance, while the separate families reflect substantial functional divergence. Ubiquitin-related proteins include covalent modifiers or ubiquitin-like domains; UBX domains are generally noncovalent adaptor domains, notably for Cdc48/p97-family ATPases; Ras-binding domains recognize Ras-family GTPases in particular signaling contexts. Cross-family structures can therefore guide modeling of the conserved beta-grasp core, but they are poor templates for family-specific interfaces or activities. It would be unsafe to annotate a UBX or Ras-binding domain as a covalently conjugated ubiquitin-like modifier, to infer proteasomal targeting or ubiquitination machinery from the shared superfamily, or to transfer p97 binding or Ras binding among these families without sequence, interface, biochemical, or cellular evidence. Even within a family, partner specificity and biological outcome require such external evidence rather than SCOPe placement alone.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
